name: Upbringing scales
licence: Written for this app and released into the public domain (CC0). The adversity list covers the standard categories used in public-health surveys of childhood adversity, in our own words.
intro: Think about home before you were 16. There are no right answers, and you can skip anything.

items.text: When I was upset, there was an adult at home who comforted me.
I was told or shown that I was loved.
The adults at home took an interest in what I was doing and how my day went.
I could talk to a parent or carer about my worries.
I felt like I was in the way at home.
Rules at home were strict and there was little room to argue.
I was shouted at when I did something wrong.
Punishments at home felt bigger than what I had done.
I was afraid of how a parent or carer would react to a mistake.
When I broke a rule, an adult explained why it mattered rather than just punishing me.
A parent or carer I lived with died, or left and did not come back.
My parents separated or divorced.
Someone at home was seriously ill, in body or mind, for a long time.
There was a lot of shouting or fighting between the adults at home.
Someone at home had a serious problem with alcohol or drugs.
I was bullied at school for a long time.
An adult who was meant to look after me hurt me, frightened me badly or kept putting me down.
There were times we did not have enough money for food, heating or rent.
We had enough money for the things we needed.
We could afford extras like holidays, clubs or lessons.
Money worries were talked about a lot at home.
Compared with other families around you, how was money at home?
How many times did you move home before you were 16?
How many times did you change school, apart from the normal move up?
The adults I lived with changed, for example a step-parent moving in or living with different relatives.
Home life was predictable: meals, bedtimes and who would be there.
As I grew up, I was allowed to make my own choices about friends, hobbies and clothes.
My opinion was asked for when the family decided things.
I was encouraged to try things by myself, even if I might fail.
A parent or carer watched me so closely that I had little privacy.
There were books, music or art around at home.
I was taken to new places and encouraged to ask questions.
An adult at home talked with me about ideas, the news or how things work.
I had at least one close friend through most of my school years.
An adult outside home, like a teacher, coach or grandparent, believed in me.
I often felt left out by other children.

birthOrder.text: Where do you come among your brothers and sisters?

adversityBands.note: Number of hard events → the model's 1–5 adversity answer. Four or more is the usual cut-off for a high-adversity childhood in public-health research.
